subject: CMO
title: The Projected Gradient Iteration
drawingCaption: Luenberger Fig. 12.4: Moving along projected negative gradient to y, followed by restoration back to constraint surface at x_{k+1}
coreTranslation: Core Algorithm: The Gradient Projection algorithm minimizes $f(x)$ over a closed convex set $\Omega$ by taking a gradient descent step into unconstrained space and immediately projecting back onto $\Omega$:
$$x_{k+1} = \Pi_\Omega\left( x_k - \alpha_k \nabla f(x_k) \right)$$

Two-Phase Interpretation (Luenberger): When constraints are linear or simple convex sets (like boxes), the projection is direct. For curved non-linear surfaces $h(x) = 0$, the algorithm takes a tangential step to $y$, followed by a normal restoration phase to reach $x_{k+1}$ on the manifold.
personalConnection: Walking down a hill on a hiking trail bounded by a wooden railing: whenever the downhill gradient points off the trail into the woods, you step forward and immediately slide along the railing, staying on the trail.
examTrap: Step size $\alpha_k$ must satisfy $\alpha_k < 2/L$ (where $L$ is the Lipschitz constant of $\nabla f$)! If $\alpha_k$ is too large, projecting back can cause iterates to bounce back and forth indefinitely across the boundary.

subject: CMO
title: Fixed-Point Characterization of Optimality
drawingSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 240 145" class="w-full h-full">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arr-1402" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="6" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 1.5 L 8 5 L 0 8.5 z" fill="#000000"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- Boundary line of Omega -->
  <line x1="30" y1="95" x2="210" y2="95" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="215" y="98" fill="#000000" font-size="9" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">∂Ω</text>
  <!-- Stationary Point x* -->
  <circle cx="120" cy="95" r="4" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="120" y="115" fill="#000000" font-size="9" font-family="serif" font-style="italic" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">x* = Π_Ω(x* - α ∇f(x*))</text>
  <!-- Outward normal gradient vector -->
  <line x1="120" y1="95" x2="120" y2="35" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#arr-1402)"/>
  <text x="125" y="42" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">-α ∇f(x*)</text>
  <!-- Projection arrow straight back down to x* -->
  <path d="M 120 35 L 120 95" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <text x="120" y="20" fill="#000000" font-size="9" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">Stationary Point ⇔ Zero Projected Gradient</text>
  <text x="120" y="136" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">Displacement vector -α ∇f points directly into normal cone N_Ω(x*)</text>
</svg>
drawingCaption: Fixed-Point Property: At a constrained stationary point x*, stepping along -α ∇f projects straight back to x*
coreTranslation: Fixed-Point Theorem: A point $x^* \in \Omega$ is a first-order stationary point of $\min_{x \in \Omega} f(x)$ if and only if for any step size $\alpha > 0$:
$$x^* = \Pi_\Omega(x^* - \alpha \nabla f(x^*))$$

The Projected Gradient Mapping: We define the projected gradient residual $G_\alpha(x) = \frac{1}{\alpha} (x - \Pi_\Omega(x - \alpha \nabla f(x)))$. Then $x^*$ is stationary if and only if $G_\alpha(x^*) = 0$.
This provides a continuous, scale-consistent stopping criterion $\|G_\alpha(x_k)\| \le \epsilon$ for constrained optimization.
personalConnection: Pressing your hand firmly against a glass window: you push forward with full force ($-\alpha \nabla f$), but the glass wall projects your hand back to its exact original contact point ($x^*$). Net motion is zero.
examTrap: Remember that unconstrained stationarity ($\nabla f(x^*) = 0$) DOES NOT HOLD on the boundary! The physical gradient $\nabla f(x^*)$ can be massive; stationarity only requires that its negative points outward into the normal cone.

subject: CMO
title: Convergence Rates: Sublinear to Linear
drawingSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 240 145" class="w-full h-full">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arr-1403" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="6" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 1.5 L 8 5 L 0 8.5 z" fill="#000000"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- Axes for convergence -->
  <line x1="35" y1="115" x2="215" y2="115" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#arr-1403)"/>
  <line x1="40" y1="120" x2="40" y2="20" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.2" marker-end="url(#arr-1403)"/>
  <text x="215" y="127" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">k</text>
  <text x="15" y="25" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">f(x_k) - f*</text>
  <!-- Convex 1/k curve -->
  <path d="M 45 40 Q 75 85 200 105" fill="none" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <text x="180" y="80" fill="#000000" font-size="8" font-family="serif">Convex: 𝒪(1/k)</text>
  <!-- Strongly convex linear convergence curve -->
  <path d="M 45 35 Q 85 95 140 114" fill="none" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2.2"/>
  <text x="145" y="60" fill="#000000" font-size="8" font-family="serif" font-weight="bold">Strongly Convex: 𝒪(ρ^k)</text>
  <text x="120" y="20" fill="#000000" font-size="9" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">Projected Gradient Matches Unconstrained GD Rates!</text>
</svg>
drawingCaption: Convergence Rates: Sublinear O(1/k) for general convex f, and geometric linear O(ρ^k) under strong convexity
coreTranslation: Remarkable Theorem: The projected gradient algorithm inherits the exact same theoretical convergence rates as unconstrained gradient descent!
Convex Objectives ($L$-Lipschitz gradient): With step size $\alpha = 1/L$, the objective error decreases at a sublinear rate: $f(x_k) - f^* \le \frac{L \|x_0 - x^*\|^2}{2k} = \mathcal{O}(1/k)$.

Strongly Convex Objectives ($m$-strongly convex): With step size $\alpha = 2/(L+m)$, the sequence converges with geometric linear rate: $\|x_k - x^*\| \le \left( \frac{L-m}{L+m} \right)^k \|x_0 - x^*\|$.
personalConnection: Sliding down a water slide with raised protective banks: the banks constrain your lateral path, but your downward velocity toward the pool decays at the exact same physical friction rate as on an open slope.
examTrap: Projection does NOT slow down asymptotic convergence rates! The only difference is the computational cost of evaluating $\Pi_\Omega(x)$ at each iteration.

subject: CMO
title: Armijo Line Search along the Projection Arc
drawingSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 240 145" class="w-full h-full">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arr-1404" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="6" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 1.5 L 8 5 L 0 8.5 z" fill="#000000"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- Feasible set boundary corner -->
  <line x1="30" y1="120" x2="120" y2="120" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2"/>
  <line x1="120" y1="120" x2="190" y2="40" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2"/>
  <!-- Curved projection arc x(α) bending along boundary -->
  <path d="M 50 120 L 120 120 L 165 70" fill="none" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <circle cx="50" cy="120" r="4" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="50" y="135" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">x_k</text>
  <!-- Accepted iterate on arc -->
  <circle cx="140" cy="98" r="3.5" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="145" y="112" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">x_k(α_k)</text>
  <text x="120" y="20" fill="#000000" font-size="9" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">Projection Arc: x(α) = Π_Ω(x_k - α ∇f(x_k))</text>
  <text x="120" y="35" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic" text-anchor="middle">f(x(α)) ≤ f(x_k) - γ ∇f(x_k)ᵀ (x_k - x(α))</text>
</svg>
drawingCaption: Projection Arc Line Search: Backtracking along the piecewise-linear boundary curve x(α) to satisfy Armijo descent
coreTranslation: In constrained optimization, stepping along a straight ray $x_k - \alpha \nabla f(x_k)$ leaves the feasible set. We must search along the Projection Arc $x(\alpha) = \Pi_\Omega(x_k - \alpha \nabla f(x_k))$.
Armijo Condition along the Arc (Bertsekas): Choose step size $\alpha = \beta^m s$ by backtracking until:
$$f(x(\alpha)) \le f(x_k) - \gamma \nabla f(x_k)^T (x_k - x(\alpha))$$
Because $x(\alpha)$ bends along the facets of $\Omega$, this non-linear arc search can change active constraints multiple times in a single iteration!
personalConnection: Navigating a sharp highway exit: you don't drive straight into the guardrail and then turn. Your car follows the curved arc of the exit ramp, smoothly shedding speed as the curve tightens.
examTrap: Do NOT evaluate the Armijo gradient test against $-\alpha \nabla f(x_k)$! You must evaluate the reduction against the actual displacement vector $x_k - x(\alpha)$, because that is the physical step taken.

subject: CMO
title: Restoration Phase for Non-Linear Manifolds
drawingSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 240 145" class="w-full h-full">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arr-1405" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="6" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 1.5 L 8 5 L 0 8.5 z" fill="#000000"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- Curved non-linear constraint surface h(x) = 0 -->
  <path d="M 40 120 Q 120 70 200 45" fill="none" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="205" y="45" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">h(x) = 0</text>
  <!-- Tangent line at x_k -->
  <line x1="50" y1="120" x2="160" y2="70" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
  <circle cx="95" cy="95" r="4" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="90" y="110" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">x_k</text>
  <!-- Tangent step point y -->
  <circle cx="150" cy="74" r="3.5" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="155" y="68" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">y (Infeasible)</text>
  <!-- Restoration arrow normal to tangent -->
  <line x1="150" y1="74" x2="160" y2="58" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#arr-1405)"/>
  <circle cx="160" cy="58" r="4" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="175" y="60" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic" font-weight="bold">x_{k+1}</text>
  <text x="120" y="20" fill="#000000" font-size="9" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">Two Phases: Tangent Step + Newton Restoration</text>
</svg>
drawingCaption: Restoration Phase: Stepping along the tangent plane leaves the curved manifold; Newton iteration restores feasibility
coreTranslation: When constraints $h_i(x) = 0$ are curved non-linear surfaces, the tangent plane $\{d : \nabla h(x_k)^T d = 0\}$ is only a first-order local approximation.
Phase 1 (Tangent Step): Take a descent step along the projected gradient on the tangent plane to point $y = x_k - \alpha_k P_k \nabla f(x_k)$. Point $y$ is slightly infeasible ($h(y) \ne 0$).

Phase 2 (Restoration): Solve the underdetermined non-linear system $h(x) = 0$ starting from $y$ using Newton's method in the normal space $ abla h(x_k)$: $x_{k+1} = y - abla h^T ( abla h abla h^T)^{-1} h(y)$.
math:
$$y = x_k - \alpha P_k 
abla f(x_k), \quad x_{k+1} = y - 
abla h(x_k) [
abla h(x_k)^T 
abla h(x_k)]^{-1} h(y) \quad (	ext{Feasibility Restored})$$
personalConnection: Walking along the equator on a globe: if you take a straight tangential step into outer space ($y$), you float off the planet. You must drop straight down along the radius (normal restoration) to plant your boots back on the curved earth ($x_{k+1}$).
examTrap: If step size $\alpha$ is chosen too large, the tangent point $y$ may fly so far from the manifold that the Newton restoration phase fails to converge (or converges to a completely different branch of the constraint surface)!

subject: CMO
title: Worked Benchmark: Projected GD on Non-Negative Orthant
drawingSvg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 240 145" class="w-full h-full">
  <defs>
    <marker id="arr-1406" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="6" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 1.5 L 8 5 L 0 8.5 z" fill="#000000"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <!-- Axes: First quadrant non-negative orthant -->
  <line x1="40" y1="120" x2="210" y2="120" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="215" y="123" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">x₁</text>
  <line x1="50" y1="125" x2="50" y2="25" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="50" y="20" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">x₂</text>
  <!-- Unconstrained step dipping into quadrant 4 -->
  <circle cx="90" cy="80" r="3.5" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="95" y="78" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif">x₀=(1, 1)</text>
  <line x1="90" y1="80" x2="140" y2="135" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.2" stroke-dasharray="2,2"/>
  <circle cx="140" cy="135" r="3" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="145" y="140" fill="#000000" font-size="7.5" font-family="serif">(2, -0.5) Infeasible</text>
  <!-- Projected coordinate-wise clipping -->
  <line x1="140" y1="135" x2="140" y2="120" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#arr-1406)"/>
  <circle cx="140" cy="120" r="4" fill="#000000"/>
  <text x="140" y="112" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="serif" font-weight="bold">x₁=(2, 0)</text>
  <text x="135" y="30" fill="#000000" font-size="8.5" font-family="sans-serif" font-weight="bold" text-anchor="middle">Projected Iteration: x_{k+1} = max(0, x_k - α ∇f(x_k))</text>
</svg>
drawingCaption: Worked Benchmark: Unconstrained step plunges below axis into quadrant 4; projection clips negative x₂ cleanly to 0
coreTranslation: Problem: Minimize $f(x) = \frac{1}{2} x_1^2 + x_2^2 - 2 x_1 + 3 x_2$ subject to $x_1 \ge 0, x_2 \ge 0$, starting from $x_0 = (1, 1)$ with step size $\alpha = 1.0$.
Step 1 (Gradient Evaluation): $\nabla f(x_0) = [x_1 - 2, \; 2x_2 + 3]^T = [1 - 2, \; 2(1) + 3]^T = [-1, \; 5]^T$.
Step 2 (Unconstrained Step): $y = x_0 - \alpha \nabla f(x_0) = [1, 1]^T - 1.0 [-1, 5]^T = [2, \; -4]^T$.
Step 3 (Projection onto $\mathbb{R}_+^2$): $x_1 = \max(0, y) = [\max(0, 2), \; \max(0, -4)]^T = (2, 0)$. Component $x_2$ hit the boundary and clamped to zero in a single step!
personalConnection: Clipping negative audio waveform samples to zero in an electronic half-wave rectifier: the negative half of the alternating current is instantly truncated flat against the zero voltage line.
examTrap: Notice how projected gradient immediately identifies active constraints! Unlike active set methods (which add constraints one-by-one), projected gradient can activate DOZENS of bound constraints simultaneously in a single iteration.
